Financing Grid Buildout: Mobilizing Capital Across Models

Clean Energy

Rising grid investment needs are pushing markets to draw on a broader range of capital sources. Traditional models that rely heavily on public sources and utility balance sheets can limit the scale and pace of network expansion, particularly where leverage is high or tariff increases are difficult. Meeting future investment needs will require mobilizing a wider investor base and, in some markets, additional delivery capacity. Globally, governments and utilities are increasingly combining public, private and development capital to support new grid infrastructure.
Both transmission and distribution require substantial investment, though transmission projects accommodate a wider range of financing structures. Transmission projects are generally larger, more discrete and easier to separate from the wider utility business, with identifiable assets, investment requirements and regulated or contracted revenue streams. These characteristics make project-level financing, leasing, concessions and independent transmission models easier to apply. Distribution investment is typically more fragmented and closely integrated with utility operations, limiting the scope for comparable structures at scale, although private debt and other financing mechanisms can still support distribution spending. This report therefore focuses on financing structures for greenfield transmission projects.
Grid financing extends well beyond direct equity investment. Models range from direct public funding and utility borrowing to public-private co-investment and independent transmission projects, using different combinations of debt, equity, concessional finance and guarantees. The appropriate model for a market depends on multiple factors, including project economics, revenue certainty, utility borrowing capacity, regulation and government preferences around ownership, control and energy security.
Private finance can increase available capital, with the degree of balance-sheet relief and risk transfer depending on the structure. Private debt can supplement public and utility financing, although borrowing raised directly by a utility still increases leverage. Project-level financing brings capital outside the utility balance sheet and ties repayment to project revenues. Private equity can provide additional risk capital, but requires governments and utilities to share or transfer asset ownership.
 Private participation can be structured without requiring permanent transfer of strategic grid assets. Joint ventures, leasing, build-transfer structures and time-limited concessions can bring in private capital while preserving public ownership or returning assets to the public sector after a defined period. Where governments are comfortable with private ownership, independent transmission projects can transfer more financing and delivery responsibilities to private investors.
Development finance is most effective where financing costs, risk allocation or access to capital are the main barriers to investment. Guarantees, concessional lending and other risk-mitigation instruments can lower financing costs, strengthen payment security and absorb sovereign, counterparty or early-stage project risks that commercial investors may be unwilling to take. Where projects are held back by permitting, weak regulation, inadequate cost recovery or institutional capacity, additional capital alone will have limited impact. Development finance can nevertheless help viable projects progress as governments undertake the broader reforms needed to make investment sustainable at scale.
A strong enabling environment is critical to turn available capital into sustained grid investment. Credible cost recovery, predictable regulation, payment security, well-prepared project pipelines, timely permitting and clear risk allocation determine whether capital can be deployed at scale. Weaknesses in these areas can deter private investment even when capital and investor appetite exist.
BNEF’s case studies illustrate how financing models vary with market structure and policy priorities. Brazil uses competitively awarded private transmission concessions supported by long-term regulated revenues. Mexico retains public ownership of the grid and supplements public funding through capital-market financing. South Korea and South Africa are at the early stages of introducing private capital into transmission delivery, with key questions around risk allocation, payment mechanisms and investor returns still being decided. For the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) power grid, the near-term challenge is developing investable projects by resolving cross-border cost sharing, commercial arrangements and delivery responsibilities.
 
Approach: This report draws on BNEF’s New Energy Outlook: Grids 2026 for forward-looking grid investment scenarios and the Grid Investment Outlook: 2025 for historical grid investment estimates. It also incorporates BNEF’s proprietary modeling of financing structures and investment needs, alongside data collected from the Bloomberg Terminal and public documents from utilities, regulators, governments, development finance institutions and other relevant sources. Case studies and analysis reflects the knowledge and expertise of BNEF’s regional and sector analysts. All data and analysis reflect information available as of October 2026.
